primers.title: A Pauli is a label plus a phase — and the label reads right-to-left
primers.body_md:
`Pauli` stores a string over I/X/Y/Z together with a phase coefficient drawn from +1, i, −1, −i. The phase can be written into the label itself with one of the prefixes `''`, `'i'`, `'-'`, `'-i'`, so `Pauli('iXX')` is a legal and *distinct* object; a plain multi-letter label carries no phase, which is why `Pauli('XZ').to_matrix()` is exactly the bare tensor product.

The rule that decides most exam points: the label is read RIGHT to LEFT against qubit indices. The rightmost character is qubit 0, the leftmost is the highest-index qubit. `Pauli('IX')` is X on qubit 0; `Pauli('XZ')` is X on qubit 1 and Z on qubit 0, whose matrix is `np.kron(X, Z)` — the same left-to-right order you would write by hand. That coincidence is the trap: the matrix looks like nothing special, so the convention stays invisible until a question asks *which qubit* an operator acts on. If you want Z on qubit 0, you write `Pauli('IZ')`, never `Pauli('ZI')`, and no method call fixes the mistake — `.adjoint()` returns Hermitian labels unchanged rather than reversing the qubit order.

Two families of combination methods, and the whole objective lives on telling them apart. Tensor: `a.tensor(b)` is a ⊗ b, putting the caller `a` on the higher-index subsystem and the argument `b` on qubit 0; `a.expand(b)` is the mirror, b ⊗ a, with `a` on subsystem 0. Product: `a.dot(b)` is the plain matrix product A·B, while `a.compose(b)` is *circuit order* — `a` acts first, so the matrix is B·A (and `compose(b, front=True)` gets you back to A·B). On Paulis the difference shows up as a single character: `Pauli('X').dot(Pauli('Y'))` is `iZ`, while `Pauli('X').compose(Pauli('Y'))` is `-iZ`. Reversing the operands conjugates the phase, and the class never silently drops it.

For observables you rarely hand-build a `Pauli` — you build a `SparsePauliOp`, a linear combination of Pauli strings, and that is what the Estimator primitive expects. `from_list` takes (label, coeff) pairs on full-width labels; `from_sparse_list` takes (label, qubit_indices, coeff) plus an explicit `num_qubits`, and there the label characters pair with the index list left-to-right — so a `"ZX"` on indices 1 and 4 of a five-qubit register prints back as `XIIZI`, the little-endian display rule read out at you. `simplify()` sums the coefficients of repeated terms (never averages them) and drops only terms whose coefficient is zero within tolerance.

Commutation is a counting exercise, not a matrix multiplication: two multi-qubit Paulis commute exactly when the number of positions at which their single-qubit factors anticommute is EVEN. X⊗X versus Z⊗Z anticommute in both positions, so they commute; X⊗I versus Z⊗Z anticommute in one, so they do not. An identity factor contributes zero to the count — it never buys commutation by itself.

primers.title: Statevector is the simulator you carry in your head
primers.body_md:
Four constructors matter. `Statevector.from_label('10')` reads the string as |q_(n−1) … q_0⟩, so '10' sets qubit 1 and puts the amplitude at index 2; it also accepts multi-character labels and the eigenstate letters '+', '−', 'r', 'l'. `Statevector.from_int(2, dims=4)` names that same state by its integer index (an int `dims` is the *total* dimension and is accepted). `Statevector.from_instruction(qc)` — and the plain constructor `Statevector(qc)`, which delegates to the same evolution — runs |0…0⟩ through a circuit. A UNITARY circuit only: leave a `measure` in and both raise `QiskitError: Cannot apply instruction with classical bits: measure`. There is no `shots=` or `backend=` escape hatch and no save-instruction workaround; delete the measurement.

Everything downstream is functional. `sv.evolve(op)` returns a NEW `Statevector` and leaves the source untouched; it accepts a `Pauli`, an `Operator`, a gate, or a circuit. Read-out then splits into two families that questions love to swap. `.data` gives complex amplitudes; `.probabilities()` gives their squared moduli as an ndarray in index order; `.probabilities_dict()` gives the same numbers keyed by bitstring; `.probabilities([0])` marginalizes over every qubit not listed and still returns an ndarray (length 2 for one qubit), not a dict. Dictionary keys follow the same q_(n−1)…q_0 order as labels, so applying X to qubit 0 of a two-qubit circuit yields the key `'01'`, not `'10'`. The identical right-is-qubit-0 rule governs `Operator(qc)`: an H on qubit 0 of a two-qubit circuit is I ⊗ H, with the acting gate on the RIGHT of the tensor product.

Gate algebra is the other half of the objective, and the phase family is where the traps sit. Z = diag(1, −1); S = diag(1, i) is the square root of Z and is literally `p(π/2)`; T = diag(1, e^(iπ/4)) is the square root of S; the daggered forms `sdg` and `tdg` carry the conjugated phase. `P(θ) = diag(1, e^(iθ))` puts the entire phase on the |1⟩ amplitude, while `RZ(θ) = diag(e^(−iθ/2), e^(+iθ/2))` splits it symmetrically — so RZ and P of the same angle differ by a global phase, never by physics. That distinction is exactly what `Operator.__eq__` and `Operator.equiv` separate: `==` compares matrix elements (approximately) and is False for Z versus RZ(π), while `.equiv` ignores a global phase and is True. A `global_phase` you set on a circuit yourself is unobservable in the same way — exact probabilities and seeded sampled counts come back bit-identical.

For rotations, two memorized formulas answer most probability questions without touching a simulator: RY(θ)|0⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + sin(θ/2)|1⟩, hence P(1) = sin²(θ/2) and ⟨Z⟩ = cos θ. Expectation values come from `sv.expectation_value(obs)`, which accepts any `Pauli` or `SparsePauliOp` — for |00⟩ against Z⊗Z + 0.5·(X⊗X) the answer is 1.0, because |00⟩ is a +1 eigenstate of ZZ while XX maps it to the orthogonal |11⟩.

facts.fact_md: Pauli labels are little-endian: `Pauli('IX')` is I ⊗ X — X on qubit 0, identity on qubit 1 — and indexing the object returns the qubit-0 factor first.
`Pauli('XZ').to_matrix()` is a 4×4 matrix equal to `np.kron(X, Z)`: X on qubit 1, Z on qubit 0, with no phase prefix in the label.
To place Z on qubit 0 you must write `Pauli('IZ')` — `Pauli('ZI')` is the opposite operator, and `.adjoint()` does not reverse qubit order (Hermitian labels come back unchanged).
`a.tensor(b)` is a ⊗ b with the CALLER on the higher-index qubit: `Pauli('X').tensor(Pauli('Y'))` has label `'XY'`. `expand` is the mirror image (b ⊗ a).
Pauli products keep their phase: X·Y = iZ, Y·Z = iX, Z·X = iY via `.dot`; reversing the operands conjugates it (Y·X = `-iZ`, Z·Y = `-iX`).
`A.compose(B)` returns the operator with matrix B·A (circuit order — A acts first); `A.compose(B, front=True)` and `A.dot(B)` give A·B.
Two multi-qubit Paulis commute iff they anticommute on an EVEN number of positions: `Pauli('XX').commutes(Pauli('ZZ'))` is True, `Pauli('XI').commutes(Pauli('ZZ'))` is False.
`SparsePauliOp.simplify()` SUMS the coefficients of duplicate terms (Z with 1 and Z with 2 becomes Z with 3) — it never averages them and never keeps only the largest.
`Statevector.from_label('10')` reads the label as |q1 q0⟩, so the amplitude 1 lands at index 2 of a 4-amplitude state.
`Statevector.from_int(2, dims=4)` accepts an integer `dims` (the total dimension) and returns the single basis state at index 2.
`probabilities_dict()` keys are q_(n−1)…q_0 bitstrings: applying X to qubit 0 of a two-qubit circuit gives the key `'01'` with probability 1.0, never `'10'` and never an integer index.
`sv.probabilities([0])` marginalizes over the other qubits and returns an ndarray of length 2 (a Bell state gives 0.5/0.5) — not a dict.
`Operator(qc)` for an H on qubit 0 of a two-qubit circuit is the 4×4 matrix I ⊗ H — qubit 0 sits on the RIGHT of the tensor product, not the left.

`Statevector.from_instruction` and `Statevector(qc)` both raise `QiskitError: Cannot apply instruction with classical bits: measure` on a measured circuit; there is no `shots`/`backend` parameter and appending a save instruction does not help.
S is the square root of Z with matrix diag(1, i) — a π/2 phase, the same operation as the phase gate `p(π/2)`.
`sdg` is what applies the −i phase: after H, `s` gives (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2 and `sdg` gives (|0⟩ − i|1⟩)/√2; `z` would give −1 and `tdg` would give e^(−iπ/4).
T = diag(1, e^(iπ/4)): on |1⟩ the statevector records [0, 0.7071+0.7071j] — Qiskit keeps the factor explicitly even though it is only a global phase there.
RZ(θ) = diag(e^(−iθ/2), e^(+iθ/2)) splits the phase: RZ(π/2)|0⟩ is [0.7071−0.7071j, 0] while the probabilities stay [1.0, 0.0].
`Operator.equiv` ignores a global phase and `==` does not: Z versus RZ(π) is equiv-True but ==-False; T versus RZ(π/2) is False both ways (that pairing is S).
For RY(θ)|0⟩ the probability of outcome 1 is sin²(θ/2) — θ = π/3 gives exactly 0.25.
For the same state ⟨Z⟩ = cos θ — at θ = π/3 the expectation value is 0.5, not sin/cos of the half angle.
Setting `qc.global_phase` changes nothing observable: exact probabilities are identical and a seeded sampling run returns the same counts as the phase-free circuit.

`efficient_su2(n, reps=r)` has `2·n·(r+1)` free parameters — an `ry` and an `rz` on every qubit, and one rotation layer MORE than `reps` because a final rotation layer follows the last entangler: `efficient_su2(4, reps=2)` gives 24, and `skip_final_rotation_layer=True` drops it to 16.

`real_amplitudes` is the RY-only sibling of `efficient_su2`: its gate set is exactly `ry` + `cx` (so `n·(reps+1)` parameters, 12 at the default reps=3 on 3 qubits), while `efficient_su2` adds the `rz` layer. `quantum_volume` carries no free parameters at all.

`QFTGate(n)` takes only a qubit count (no `do_swaps`, no `approximation_degree` — those belonged to the deprecated `QFT` class). One `decompose()` opens it into n `h`, n(n−1)/2 `cp` and ⌊n/2⌋ `swap`: for n = 4 that is `{'h': 4, 'cp': 6, 'swap': 2}`, never `cx` (translating `cp` to a hardware basis is the transpiler's job).
